analysis.one_liner: Makes schools legally liable for sexual harassment of students and opens the courthouse doors for victims to sue for damages.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Debbie Dingell with 5 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or further action before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current Supreme Court rulings, a student who is sexually harassed at school can generally win money damages from the school only if a school official actually knew about the harassment and then failed to respond. This bill would reverse that standard: schools would be liable for harassment by an employee that was enabled by that employee's authority, even if the school never knew about it, and for harassment the school knew or should have known about. It would also explicitly guarantee every student the right to sue for damages, including punitive damages and attorney's fees, and would spell out the steps a school must take to avoid liability, such as publicizing a complaint process and providing supportive measures to the victim.
analysis.who_benefits: Students, families, and others participating in federally funded education programs — especially girls, LGBTQ students, students with disabilities, and students of color, who the bill's findings say experience harassment at elevated rates. Victims of harassment by teachers, coaches, or other school employees would be able to recover compensation without having to prove school administrators personally knew about the misconduct, and every victim of Title IX discrimination would gain a guaranteed right to sue in court.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students harassed in schools and colleges

how_it_helps.text: The bill would hold a school liable for sexual harassment by an employee that was enabled by the employee's authority and created a hostile environment, 'regardless of whether the entity knew or should have known about such conduct,' removing the actual-notice requirement the Supreme Court imposed in Gebser v. Lago Vista.

It would allow any person aggrieved by a covered entity's failure to comply with Title IX to bring a civil action, and would let plaintiffs recover compensatory and punitive damages, attorney's fees, and expert fees — remedies courts have made hard to obtain for students.

It would spell out a school's path to avoiding liability: an effective, publicized harassment policy; prompt and impartial investigations when requested or needed; supportive measures that preserve the victim's access to education; and corrective action, regardless of whether the victim suffered subsequent harassment.

The bill's findings state that courts had made standards for student harassment lawsuits more onerous than workplace standards under Title VII, meaning students had to suffer worse harassment than adult employees before getting a remedy; the bill would restore the full range of remedies Congress intended.

analysis.who_pays: Schools, colleges, and universities receiving federal funds would face greater liability exposure — settlements, judgments, and the cost of stronger prevention policies, staffing for investigations, and insurance. Those costs could ultimately be passed to taxpayers and tuition payers, and schools argue broader liability can drive defensive, overreaching discipline. Liability insurers serving education institutions would also bear higher risk.

drawbacks.text: The strictest provision would make schools liable for employee harassment they had no knowledge of, so a district could pay damages even after acting on every complaint it ever received; schools and their insurers would respond with higher insurance costs, and some of those costs would fall on taxpayers and students through tuition and fees.

Broad liability with punitive damages gives schools an incentive to over-suppress accusations — automatically removing accused employees and suspending accused students — which civil-liberties advocates argue can deny accused people fair process, a concern that has shaped the Title IX rulemakings the bill's findings criticize.
The right to sue for punitive damages in federal court could produce lengthy litigation against school districts, diverting money and administrative attention from classrooms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For survivors, the change is substantial: it removes a standard that, in practice, lets schools avoid damages unless a specific official actually knew of the harassment. The main costs are financial — higher liability exposure and insurance for schools — and a real risk of overcorrecting in disciplinary procedures. The bill includes a school-side safe harbor (an effective policy plus prompt response) that softens the exposure for non-employee and unknown harassment, though it deliberately offers no such escape for employee harassment enabled by the employee's authority.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, which never scheduled it for a hearing or vote, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Debbie Dingell introduced the bill in the House on September 28, 2021, together with Rep. Jahana Hayes, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
Five House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

No further action — no committee markup, hearing vote, or floor action — appears in the bill's action history, and the bill was never reported out of committee before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Schools, colleges, universities, and their liability insurers are better off, because the stricter harassment liability standards and guaranteed right to sue were never enacted; students who face harassment under current court standards gain nothing.

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House on September 28, 2021.

for.name: 5 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill after its introduction.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote, so no roll calls exist; its sponsors and all five cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican support is recorded.

industries.note: The bill would make institutions strictly liable for harassment by employees enabled by their authority, even without school knowledge, and guarantee a right to sue for punitive damages. Their interest in limiting liability ran against the bill's protections for harassed students.
Districts would face the same expanded liability and would need to fund stronger prevention policies, investigations, and supportive measures for victims.
Greater exposure to damages verdicts and settlements would raise claims and premiums for insurers covering schools and colleges.
